::: {.chapter-lead}
This page is the third stop (3 of 5) of the guided tour. The block is the repeated unit of the network. This page follows the file line by line, from parameter initialization to the full `forward`. Source: [`src/llm_lab/foundations/transformer_block.py`](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/src/llm_lab/foundations/transformer_block.py#L50-L186).
:::
::: {.callout-tip title="The Transformer block in one minute" #revision-summary}
The reference block follows a pre-LN order: normalize, compute multi-head self-attention, add the residual path, then normalize, apply the MLP, and add its residual. Q/K/V/O projections and tensor shapes make the computation traceable; MQA/GQA, MLA and local attention are compared as architectural variants, not claimed as implemented in this code.
:::

::: {.callout-note .learning-outcomes collapse="true" title="Learning outcomes"}
By the end of this tour, you will be able to:
- trace a `(B, T, d)` shape through the block, from input to output;
- explain why normalization sits inside the branch instead of on the residual trunk;
- describe the role of each Q, K, V and O projection, and why heads stay isolated until `w_o`;
- distinguish MHA, MQA, GQA, MLA, and local/sparse attention by the factor each one changes.
:::

## The block's recipe: pre-LN with residuals {#block-recipe}

```python
x = x + self._attention(layer_norm(x, self.ln1_gamma, self.ln1_beta))
return x + self._mlp(layer_norm(x, self.ln2_gamma, self.ln2_beta))
```

The block applies two **additive** updates to the same stream `x`:

1. `x + attention(ln(x))` — the attention branch;
2. `x + mlp(ln(x))` — the MLP branch.

Normalization sits **inside the branch**, not on the identity path. This path lets the input bypass the sublayer directly; its output is then added to the correction computed by the branch. This structure facilitates signal and gradient propagation, but the addition does not guarantee that every input component is preserved. This is GPT-2's **pre-LN** order. This placement is often more favorable for optimizing deep Transformers: Xiong et al. (2020) find, in their theoretical and experimental setting, better-behaved gradients at initialization than with post-LN, which can reduce the need for learning-rate *warm-up*. This does not guarantee universal stability or superiority; those also depend on the architecture, initialization, and training protocol. [Xiong et al. (2020), *On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/xiong20b.html).

## Initializing: why `rng` is an argument

```python
    def __init__(self, config: GPTConfig, rng: np.random.Generator) -> None:
        d = config.embedding_dim
        self.num_heads = config.num_heads
        self.head_dim = d // config.num_heads
```

- The `rng` generator is supplied by the model and shared in stacking order: parameters become a **deterministic function of the configuration**.
- `head_dim = d // H`: each head owns `d/H` contiguous columns — the slice bounds are recomputed in `_attention`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="GPT-2-specific initialization detail"}
The GPT-2 scheme keeps the base standard deviation $0.02$ for internal projections (Q, K, V and the MLP's first layer), and reduces it for the **two output projections added to the residual stream**: attention $W_O$ and the MLP's second layer (`fc2`).

```python
residual_std = 0.02 / math.sqrt(2.0 * config.num_layers)
```

The factor $1/\sqrt{2L}$ accounts for the two residual contributions per block across $L$ blocks. It reduces the initial scale of these two output projections; it does not guarantee constant residual-stream variance. The other projections retain the base standard deviation $0.02$.
:::

Parameter creation follows: normalizations start at identity (`gamma` ones, `beta` zeros), then four `(d, d)` matrices for the Q, K, V and O projections, and two matrices for the MLP (`d -> mlp_hidden_dim -> d`).

## Attention: explicit loops, not by accident {#attention-sublayer}

```python
        q = linear(x, self.w_q, self.b_q)
        k = linear(x, self.w_k, self.b_k)
        v = linear(x, self.w_v, self.b_v)

        mask = causal_mask(seq_len)
        attended = np.empty_like(x)
        for b in range(batch):
            for h in range(self.num_heads):
                columns = slice(h * self.head_dim, (h + 1) * self.head_dim)
                head_out, _ = scaled_dot_product_attention(
                    q[b, :, columns], k[b, :, columns], v[b, :, columns], mask=mask
                )
                attended[b, :, columns] = head_out
        return linear(attended, self.w_o, self.b_o)
```

Line by line:

- Q, K, V are three projections **of the same `x`**; each shape goes from `(B, T, d)` to `(B, T, d)`.
- `causal_mask(seq_len)` lets position `i` attend to `j <= i`; future positions receive `-inf` (zero weight after softmax).
- `columns = slice(h * head_dim, (h+1) * head_dim)`: head `h` works on its own columns — a **slice**, not a copy. The multi-head split is pure column bookkeeping over the same `d`.
- Each `(b, h)` pair solves **one single-head attention problem** of shape `(T, head_dim)` — exactly the problem solved by the tested `scaled_dot_product_attention`. The explicit loops keep every intermediate shape inspectable (milestone G4's clarity-over-speed choice).
- Heads never mix until the output projection `w_o`, which alone blends information across heads.

### Single-head primitive contract

The NumPy primitive is called separately for each `(b, h)` pair. Its contract is:

- Q: `(T_q, d_k)`; K: `(T_k, d_k)`; V: `(T_k, d_v)`.
- Scores and weights: `(T_q, T_k)`; aggregated output: `(T_q, d_v)`.
- `T_q` and `T_k` may differ; so may `d_k` and `d_v`. Keys and values must share the same key-sequence length `T_k`.
- The optional additive mask has exactly shape `(T_q, T_k)`. It accepts finite biases and `-inf` to forbid an interaction; `NaN` and `+inf` are rejected.

**An edge case that must not be interpreted as a distribution:** if a row is fully masked, the primitive deliberately returns zero weights and a zero output. Rows with at least one accessible key are normalized over those keys only. This convention belongs to the reference implementation; do not generalize it to every attention API.

The [test_attention.py suite](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/tests/unit/test_attention.py) checks, among other things, shapes and normalization invariants, a hand-computable weighted sum, finite additive biases, rejection of invalid masks, the fully masked-row case, causal-mask polarity, and prefix invariance under changes to future tokens. In particular, it covers [causal-mask structure](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/tests/unit/test_attention.py#L13-L34) and [shape, normalization, and causal-invariance checks](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/tests/unit/test_attention.py#L229-L270).

Maintained sources: [NumPy primitive](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/src/llm_lab/foundations/attention.py#L9-L128) · [primitive and causal-mask tests](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/tests/unit/test_attention.py).

## Attention variants: what actually changes {#attention-variants}

The reference block above implements **standard multi-head attention (MHA)**: each head has its own Q, K, and V projections. Modern variants do not all change the same thing. Some share K/V heads to reduce the cache; others compress what is stored or restrict which positions can be attended to.

### 1. MHA, MQA, and GQA: sharing K/V heads

Let $H_q$ be the number of query heads and $H_{KV}$ the number of key/value heads.

| Variant | Query heads Q | Key/value heads K/V | Idea |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **MHA** | $H_q$ | $H_{KV}=H_q$ | Every Q head has its own K and V heads. |
| **MQA** | $H_q$ | $H_{KV}=1$ | All Q heads share one K/V head. |
| **GQA** | $H_q$ | $1 < H_{KV} < H_q$ | Q heads are partitioned into groups; each group shares K/V. |

Q remains specific to each query head. What distinguishes MQA and GQA is sharing the K/V projections and states — not removing Q heads. GQA interpolates between MHA and MQA; the number of K/V heads is an architectural choice, not a free switch applied to an already-trained model.

For dense attention with a KV cache, an approximate model-wide cache size is:
 One estimate is $M_{KV}\approx 2 L B T H_{KV} d_h b$.
where $L$ is the number of attention layers, $B$ the batch size, $T$ the retained context, $d_h$ the dimension of one KV head, and $b$ the number of bytes per element. The factor 2 stores both K and V. With dimensions and precision held fixed, moving from 32 KV heads (MHA) to 8 (GQA) therefore divides this cache by 4; moving to one (MQA) divides it by 32. This ratio applies to the K/V cache, not total model memory or necessarily measured latency.

### 2. MLA: jointly compressing K and V into a latent space

**Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)** does more than choose fewer KV heads. In DeepSeek-V2, K/V information is projected into a lower-rank latent representation that is cached during decoding; the required components are reconstructed by projection. The design described in the paper also uses a decoupled RoPE path for positional information.

The goal is to reduce the amount of KV state retained without simply replacing all heads with one shared head. The cost depends on latent dimensions, projections, kernels, and how the runtime absorbs certain projections. **Do not compare MLA with GQA only by counting KV heads**: the cached representation is different.

### 3. Local windows and sparse attention: restricting the positions being read

These methods change the **connectivity pattern**:

- **Sliding-window attention**: each position attends only to a local window of a chosen size. Attention work per position is then tied to that window rather than the entire context, but distant information is not directly accessible within one local layer.
- **Sparse or block-sparse attention**: only selected positions or blocks are allowed. Depending on the pattern, some long-range connections may remain; “sparse” therefore does not necessarily mean “strictly local.”
- **Dense global attention**: all positions permitted by the causal mask remain accessible. FlashAttention can accelerate this dense operation by reducing memory transfers without changing its mathematical connectivity pattern.

Restricting attended positions is not the same as sharing K/V heads: GQA and a local window can be combined, as illustrated by Mistral 7B. Keep three axes separate: **KV-state size**, **number of position pairs computed**, and **memory-transfer cost**.

### What this implementation does — and does not do

The NumPy code in this walkthrough is a pedagogical MHA example: $H_{KV}=H_q$, separate K/V projections per head, and dense causal attention. It does not implement GQA/MQA sharing, an inference-time KV cache, MLA latent compression, or a sparse pattern. The tables above describe distinct architectural choices; they do not claim that the reference code executes them.

**Primary sources and visual comparison:** [MHA — Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) · [MQA — Shazeer (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150) · [GQA — Ainslie et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245) · [MLA — DeepSeek-V2 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434) · [Sliding window — Mistral 7B (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06825) · [Sparse/local — Longformer (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05150) · [Visual guide to attention variants — Sebastian Raschka](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/visual-attention-variants).

## The MLP: widen, activate, project back

```python
    def _mlp(self, x: FloatArray) -> FloatArray:
        hidden = gelu(linear(x, self.w_fc1, self.b_fc1))
        return linear(hidden, self.w_fc2, self.b_fc2)
```

Each position goes on its own through `d -> mlp_hidden_dim` (often `4d`), then GELU, then back to `d`. The intermediate widening gives each position a larger space in which to compute its non-linear transformation.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Common misconceptions.** (1) "Heads see what the others do": no — each head is isolated until `w_o`. (2) "Normalization is cosmetic": no — placing it inside the branch leaves the residual path direct. Its optimization effects have been studied, including by Xiong et al. (2020); they are not a configuration-independent guarantee.
:::

## What the tests verify

[`tests/unit/test_transformer_block.py`](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/tests/unit/test_transformer_block.py#L23-L85): `forward` preserves the shape and stays finite; a non-3D input is rejected; a head count inconsistent with the width is rejected.
